message.content:
### Killing Visual Studio Code (`code.exe`) from the Command Prompt

Visual Studio Code runs as a Windows executable named **`code.exe`**.  
If you need to terminate it (and optionally its child processes) from a command line, you can use the built‑in `taskkill` utility.

#### Basic command

```cmd
taskkill /IM code.exe /F
```

- `/IM` – specifies the image name (process name).  
- `/F` – forces termination (equivalent to “kill” in Unix).

This will immediately stop all running instances of `code.exe`.

#### Terminate child processes as well

VS Code may spawn helper processes (e.g., extensions, debugging).  
To kill those too:

```cmd
taskkill /IM code.exe /F /T
```

- `/T` – terminates the specified process and any child processes started by it.

#### Find the Process ID (PID) first

If you prefer to target a specific instance (useful when multiple VS Code windows are open), first list the processes:

```cmd
tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq code.exe"
```

This will output something like:

```
Image Name                     PID Session Name        Session#    Mem Usage
========================= ======== ================ =========== ============
code.exe                    12345 Console                    1     200,000 K
```

Then kill that particular PID:

```cmd
taskkill /PID 12345 /F
```

#### Using PowerShell

If you’re in PowerShell, you can achieve the same with:

```powershell
Stop-Process -Name code -Force
```

or to include child processes:

```powershell
Get-Process code | Stop-Process -Force
```

---

### Quick Reference

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `taskkill /IM code.exe /F` | Force‑kill all VS Code instances |
| `taskkill /IM code.exe /F /T` | Force‑kill all VS Code instances + child processes |
| `tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq code.exe"` | List all VS Code processes with PIDs |
| `taskkill /PID <pid> /F` | Force‑kill a specific VS Code instance |
| `Stop-Process -Name code -Force` | PowerShell equivalent |

**Tip:** If you’re running into permission issues, try opening the Command Prompt or PowerShell as an administrator.
